title: Choose time travel, restore, checkpoints or log maintenance
brief: Time travel reads an old state, restore publishes a new state, and checkpoints accelerate state reconstruction. These operations solve different lifecycle tasks.

choices.choose_when: You want an historical read without changing head
Current head should reflect an earlier state
choices.tradeoff: Creates a new commit; missing files and protocol constraints matter

choices.choose_when: You need a checkpoint for log reconstruction
choices.tradeoff: Does not compact user data or restore removed bytes

choices.choose_when: Inspect recorded commit metadata for diagnostics/recovery
choices.tradeoff: History availability is limited by retained log state

claims.statement: Restoring v0 from a table at v1 produced v2 with the original row; v1 still selected the two-row historical state in the fixture.
Creating a checkpoint preserved the current relation in the local fixture.
Data compaction, log checkpointing, log cleanup and vacuum have different inputs and physical effects; select the intended layer.

implementation: Record version before/after restore, and test historical data availability independently.
Use history and application commit metadata for diagnosis without treating them as an indefinitely retained audit log.
errors: An old version may have loadable metadata but unavailable files; restoration has its own missing-file policy.
unknowns: Every checkpoint format and cleanup/retention combination is not covered by the fixture.

evidence.scope: Exact git-capture full contracts for the selected operations
Pinned delta-rs implementation; full file retained with acquisition provenance
Named local assertions only; see profile, fixtures and source digests

async fn load_version(&mut self, version: Version) -> Result<(), DeltaTableError>
